# Inventory vocabulary primer

## Estate config at a glance

Pulse is driven by one declarative estate-config YAML that you edit. It targets schema major v1. You never touch a host to change monitoring — you edit this file and re-render (see the invariants guide). The reference estate under `examples/reference/estate/estate.yaml` is the worked example this pack teaches from.

## Top-level sections

The estate-config declares these top-level sections (schema order):
- `estate`: Estate-wide identity and defaults — the fleet name plus fallbacks other sections inherit.
- `hosts`: The machines under management, each tagged with a collection_class that fixes how Pulse reaches and probes it.
- `services`: The workloads to watch on those hosts — what 'healthy' means and which probes prove it.
- `channels`: Where alerts are delivered (chat, email, webhook), referenced by name from routing.
- `routing_overrides`: Per-target exceptions to default severity routing — send a given entity's alerts to a specific channel.
- `suppressions`: Deliberate, rationale-bearing silences — an entity is intentionally unmonitored for a stated reason.

## Host collection classes

Every host declares exactly one collection class, which fixes how Pulse collects from it:
- `excluded`
- `hypervisor-api`
- `managed-linux`
- `nas-api`
- `probe-only`

Pick the class that matches how the host exposes itself (a Linux exporter, a hypervisor/NAS API, a black-box probe, or an explicit exclusion).

## Deep-health & backup-freshness

A service may declare a `deep_health` probe (endpoint + response_mapping + alert_expression) or a `backup_freshness` spec (signal + threshold). In the reference estate the `portal-web` service attaches a `deep_health` probe and `nas-backups` attaches a `backup_freshness` spec — copy those shapes:

```yaml
services:
  - name: portal-web
    host: harbor-web-01
    kind: http
    deep_health:
      endpoint: https://portal.aurora.example/api/health
      alert_expression: pulse_deep_health_status == 0
      credential: ${WEB_HEALTH_TOKEN}   # env reference, never a literal
```

## Command signals (host-computed backup freshness)

A `backup_freshness` spec with a `threshold` alone is a declaration-only alert threshold — it delivers no live series. Add a **`command`** and Pulse delivers it through the command-exporter: the renderer synthesizes a `scalar` command-signal on the service's host emitting `pulse_backup_freshness_age_seconds{service}` (the value) and `pulse_backup_freshness_up{service}` (`1` ok / `0` blind — missing data is never a healthy backup). The command must be read-only argv (run verbatim, no shell) that prints the age of the newest backup artifact, in **seconds**, to stdout. The service must resolve to a `managed-linux` host — that is the only class that runs the command-exporter bundle; a `command` on any other class is a validation error.

```yaml
services:
  - name: nas-backups
    host: backup-orchestrator-01          # must be a managed-linux host
    kind: backup
    backup_freshness:
      signal: pulse_backup_freshness_age_seconds
      threshold: "24h"
      command: ["/opt/pulse/backup-age", "/mnt/backups"]  # prints newest-backup AGE in seconds
      interval: "15m"                     # optional; default 15m
```

## Channels, routing & suppressions

Channels carry a credential reference and define where alerts go. Each channel has a `kind` (`chat`, `email`, `push`, `telegram`, or `webhook`). A `telegram` channel adds one required non-secret knob — `options.chat_id` (an int64 chat id or `@name`) — alongside its credential; the renderer emits it to an Alertmanager `telegram_configs` receiver with the credential as `bot_token` and `chat_id` carried verbatim from `options`. `routing_overrides` map a severity to specific channels. A `suppressions` entry silences a target, but every suppression requires an explicit `rationale` — silence is never anonymous (see the invariants guide).

```yaml
channels:
  - name: ops-telegram
    kind: telegram
    credential: ${TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN}   # bot token — a reference, never a literal
    options:
      chat_id: "-1001234567890"        # required for telegram; non-secret
```

## Layers: generated base + hand-authored overlay

A source file may carry an optional top-level `layer:` so a machine-generated skeleton and hand-authored monitoring policy live side by side in the same estate directory. `layer: base` is the regenerable, deterministic skeleton (intrinsic facts a generator knows — hosts, addresses); `layer: overlay` is the human-owned refinement. The loader deep-merges them by identity (same host/service/channel `name`, or the `estate` block) with the **overlay winning** every conflict — except a conflicting array (e.g. `exporter_ports`), where the overlay array replaces the base array whole. `layer:` is opt-in: a repo with no markers behaves exactly as before (every source implicitly `base`, a duplicate identity still a hard error). Commit the base, the overlay, and the rendered tree together, and gate with `pulse render --check` (exit 0 = the committed tree still equals a fresh render).

```yaml
# estate/00-skeleton.base.yaml — machine-generated, regenerable
layer: base
hosts:
  - name: app-01
    collection_class: managed-linux
    exporter_ports: [9100]
---
# estate/10-monitoring.overlay.yaml — you own this by hand
layer: overlay
hosts:
  - name: app-01              # same identity → deep-merged onto the base host
    cadvisor: true            # overlay scalar wins
    exporter_ports: [9100, 9256]   # overlay array REPLACES the base array whole
```

## Secret grammar

Credentials are ALWAYS a reference — `${ENV_VAR}` or `op://vault/item/field` — never an inline secret literal. If you ever see a raw token or password in a file, stop and flag it to the operator.
